waits until the ship has gone ($04, set by $6D66), then sets up the explosions and the tune ($6F2D) and makes $6D7D the interrupt's stage

waits until the explosions have played 50 times ($04, set by $6D7D); the interrupt then plays only the music ($6DAC) while the text is set up ($6F6E), and then shows the text's sprites ($6DB2)

the text is over: waits for SPACE (bit 4 of $DC01) while the tune plays, then fades it out, the volume from 15 down to 0 a step at a time, stops it ($A403), blanks the screen and goes to the game's game over at $092B, which loads the title and its hall of fame. The level the game over keeps for the table is read from the level header's place at $8CA2 and $8CA4; in this part those are bytes of the picture, $65 and $55, which the title draws as "!", so a finished game is listed at LEVEL !-!

the band of sprites now hidden at the top ($7032) gets the next two lines of text: the band's first sprite's address from its pointer ($7032 times 64, in the bank at $C000), the first line at its top and the second 13 rows down ($27 bytes on). The end mark $D3 stops the text ($05)

draws a line of text into a band of eight sprites, three characters to a sprite, from the text at ($D3). A carriage return ($0D) fills the rest of the line with spaces; a small letter ($61 to $7A) takes the font's character 96 places lower ($01 to $1A), as in the machine's own lower-case set. It draws 25 characters, but the 25th lands on the 24th's place ($703B, $7054) and is not taken from the text, so it is read again as the next line's first. Every line in the text is 24 characters, and each begins and ends with a space, so nothing shows of it; a carriage return at that place is taken there, which is why each paragraph ends with two of them for one blank line
one character from the text

After $89 it starts again at $80, held for a random 1 to 16 frames (the timer at $DC04). After 50 explosions in all ($09), $04 is set and the sprites stop changing. Then the music ($A400)

each frame: a cue or a song asked for starts first; while playing, on the frame after a step every voice reads its next row ($A6A3); on the other frames the speed counts down, every voice's sound goes on ($A876), and one frame before a step the patterns may move on ($AB6F). one voice's row: a held cue counts its rows down, and at 0 frees the voice silenced; otherwise when the row's wait is over the next row is read: its note byte (0 an empty row, $80 a release, bit 7 a new instrument), a second byte of program (high four bits) and instrument (low four), and, when the pattern's rows carry lengths, a third byte for how many steps the row lasts. A $FF after it marks the pattern's end
a note: in a shared pattern (bit 7 of the pattern number) the note goes to this voice and the next by turns, unless the next is busy
the note, transposed; its program and instrument with their offsets added; the instrument loaded if bit 7 was set ($A7B9); the voice's slide, vibrato and pulse counters cleared

loads instrument A, an entry of up to 16 bytes from $A434: attack and decay, sustain and release, the pulse sweep's rate (high four bits plus 1) with bit 0 asking for the pulse to be set even when the instrument has not changed, the pulse width and its limit, the sweep step (two bytes), the vibrato's width, delay, step and growth, a fine tuning, and, unless the twelfth byte is $FF, the filter: mode and sweep step, resonance and voices, cutoff, and frames up and down. Restarts the voice's program
the pulse width: the high four bits of its byte the high byte and, flipped, the limit; the low four times 16 the low byte; then the step
the vibrato, fine tuning and filter

the program waits a frame
